source.title: Can Transformers Learn Sequential Function Classes In Context?
source.authors: Ryan Campbell; E. Guo; Evan Hu; Reya Vir; E. Hsiao

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether in-context performance depends on context-example quality by evaluating sequential toy-task models with randomized context outputs or labels; it does not measure induction heads or training-time emergence.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses induction heads in related work and proposes measuring them in future work, but reports no induction-head measurements. Its training-loss figures do not measure the claimed token-index loss pattern or its timing relative to induction-head formation. The relevant reported results concern in-context performance under randomized context examples.
record.test_reason: The study never identifies, measures or ablates induction heads, and never tracks training dynamics. Its results are about trained toy GPT-2-style models' in-context performance on sequential function classes, with context outputs or labels randomized at evaluation time. Evaluation-time corruption of context is not a property of the training data or setup, so it does not bear on V5, which concerns whether induction heads form or ICL persists depending on training data or setup. Induction heads appear only in related work and future work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that small GPT-2-architecture transformers can learn sequential non-textual function classes in context. They find that randomizing context labels degrades ICL, but 'not to the extent one might expect', with ICL persisting below about half the labels randomized. They hypothesize that ICL mechanisms differ between textual and non-textual tasks, and leave induction-head analysis to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains toy GPT-2-architecture models on sequential function classes and evaluates them with randomized context examples; it does not reproduce the original induction-head measurements or training-dynamics analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance changes with the number of randomized context outputs or labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Toy GPT-2 models trained on sequential non-textual function classes learn in context. Their query loss rises as more context outputs or labels are randomized at evaluation, but ICL persists when fewer than half the labels are randomized.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context learners trained on structured non-textual sequential tasks are sensitive to corrupted demonstrations, unlike reports for text LMs (Min et al. 2022). This is about robustness of ICL to demonstration quality, not induction heads.

record.problems: The experiments use toy models and function classes, and the study does not measure induction heads. The relevant plotted results are described qualitatively without numerical values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows omitted. Training-loss plots and appendix plot captions were not catalogued because they do not report the claim's induction-head or token-index-loss measures; cited findings from other work are not this study's results.

untested.parts: No identification of induction or previous-token heads, and no composition or [A][B]…[A]→[B] test.
No tracking of head formation, abruptness, ICL gain or loss bump over training.
No attribution of ICL to induction heads, and no large models.
Induction behaviour is not measured in any model.
No manipulation of training data or setup, and no measure of induction-head formation or of ICL persistence over training. Only evaluation-time context corruption is tested.
No test separating few-shot task learning from copying mechanisms.
No analysis of formation sub-steps or transitions.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its V5 'supports' label are rejected. The randomization is an evaluation-time perturbation, so it says nothing about training-data dependence of induction-head formation. The paper is a student project preprint with no numeric values or uncertainty for the randomization results.

versions.untested_parts: No induction-head identification, composition, or [A][B] … [A] → [B] test.
No measurement of induction-head formation over training, abruptness, token-index in-context learning gain, or a corresponding loss bump.
No test of induction heads as the mechanism behind most in-context learning, and no large-transformer or token-index-loss evaluation.
The models use non-textual sequential tasks, but the study does not test for induction behaviour across models, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.

Tests the effect of randomized context examples on in-context performance in a toy sequential task; does not test whether or when induction heads form, or whether their formation depends on training data or setup.
No few-shot task-learning test that distinguishes copying from other heads or mechanisms.
No analysis of induction-head formation or separate transitions.

rows.measure: Squared error of the query output; qualitative in-context prediction performance
rows.value: The text states that increasing the number of randomized context outputs makes successful next-output prediction harder.
rows.note: The text reports the direction of the effect but gives no plotted numerical values.
rows.check: Randomized context outputs are applied at evaluation, not in training. The row measures ICL robustness to corrupted context, not induction-head formation or a training-data dependence, so it bears on no version. The direction is stated only qualitatively and no numbers are given.

rows.measure: Squared loss of the query output; whether in-context learning still occurs
rows.value: The text states that in-context learning still occurs when fewer than half of the total in-context examples have randomized labels.
rows.note: The text also says performance degrades with randomized labels, but supplies no numerical value for this condition.
rows.check: Label permutation is applied at evaluation, so the row does not test V5's training-data dependence. Baseline is not stated. stage_stated copies the paper's inconsistent mention of 'linear functions' although the task is recursive ReLU networks. The text also says performance degrades overall, which the value omits.

reader_labels.condition: Randomized context outputs or labels in the tested toy sequential-task settings
reader_labels.reason: More randomized context outputs make prediction harder, while in-context learning persists with label randomization below half the examples; these results show context setup affects performance (r1, r2).
